title: Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT) on Students’ Critical Thinking Skills and Academic Integrity in Higher Education
authors: Seemeen Umar Khan Yousufzai; Zunaira Faraz; Muhammad Junaid Abbad; Syed Tahir Ali Shah
source_used: OpenAlex abstract (api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.70670/sra.v4i1.1865); oa_url timed out; OpenAlex PDF location pointed to a different paper (PJSSR, different authors) and was not used

key_findings.finding: ChatGPT usage was negatively associated with both critical thinking and academic integrity scores in regression (reported betas -0.32 and -0.28).

dimensions.integrity_security: Higher self-reported ChatGPT use associated with lower self-reported integrity adherence.

author_recommendations: Structured guidelines and AI literacy programmes for responsible use (not tested)
limitations: Self-report cross-sectional survey; abstract only, so sampling and context details could not be checked.

quality.note: Abstract only; design is correlational self-report.

redesign_note: Offers only attitude/usage correlations; nothing directly on how assessment should be redesigned.

title: Examining the Threat of ChatGPT to the Validity of Short Answer Assessments in an Undergraduate Medical Program
authors: Leo Morjaria; Levi Burns; Keyna Bracken; Quang Ngo; Mark Lee; Anthony J Levinson
venue: Journal of Medical Education and Curricular Development
source_used: PubMed Central full text (PMC10540597)
ft_reason: HE medical programme; tests ChatGPT on real short-answer assessments with blinded tutor marking; GenAI; peer-reviewed 2023.
study_design: Blinded comparative evaluation (ChatGPT vs student answers marked by tutors)
sample: 40 concept application exercise questions (30 ChatGPT-3.5 answers, 10 minimally passing student answers), marked by 6 tutors; McMaster University, Canada

key_findings.finding: ChatGPT-3.5 averaged 3.29/5, above minimally passing students (2.38) but below the historical cohort mean on the same questions (3.67).
When tutors guessed authorship, 36% of guesses wrongly judged ChatGPT answers to be human-written, and inter-rater agreement was low (Fleiss kappa 0.137-0.189).
key_findings.location: Results: Free-text tutor comments; Interrater reliability

dimensions.capability_verification: A passing AI answer undermines the inference that a pass shows student competence.
dimensions.integrity_security: ChatGPT passed short-answer assessments, and tutors could not reliably identify AI-written answers.

author_recommendations: Reconsider unsupervised short-answer formats in light of GenAI capability (not tested)
limitations: Small sample, GPT-3.5 only, image questions excluded, and a single institution.

quality.note: Clear blinded design with limitations stated.

redesign_note: Shows that an unsupervised short-answer format is vulnerable and that markers cannot detect AI answers.

title: Assessment design under imperfect information: generative AI, disclosure, and student response in higher education

redesign_note: Provides a design matrix and theory for aligning disclosure, monitoring and task design.

title: The Disclosure-Detection Nexus in Generative AI: An Integrated Analysis of Ethical Implications in Academia

sample: 190 records identified (EBSCOhost, Taylor & Francis, institutional repositories), screened to a final set (Fig 1)

key_findings.finding: Current AI detection tools are unreliable and biased, and their false positives erode trust; the review therefore favours disclosure as proactive and detection as only responsive.
Recommends redesigning assessment towards oral exams, real-world cases and process-based tasks, and suggests interviewing students rather than relying on detector scores.

dimensions.integrity_security: Detector unreliability and bias argue against punitive detection.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Robust disclosure is the proactive core of integrity.

author_recommendations: Redesign assessments towards oral, case-based and process-based tasks (not tested)
limitations: Subjective thematic interpretation and limited databases (Sec 6).

quality.note: Review method described; limitations section present.

redesign_note: Synthesises the limits of detection and the role of disclosure, which redesign must respond to.

title: From adoption to accountable integration in nursing higher education: A SAFE-GenAI framework for nurse academics
authors: Zenas B. Paloma; Joanna Ruth S. Paloma
source_used: Semantic Scholar abstract (Elsevier closed; OpenAlex had no abstract)
ft_reason: Discussion paper proposing a general framework for accountable GenAI integration in nursing education; assessment is one sub-element (Amendment 3: c).
sample: Not applicable

key_findings.finding: Proposes SAFE-GenAI (stewardship, alignment, facilitation, evaluation, with equity cross-cutting); alignment covers fit of GenAI use with learning outcomes, assessment and professional standards.

dimensions.lo_alignment: Alignment domain links GenAI use to learning outcomes and assessment.

author_recommendations: Use SAFE-GenAI to guide curriculum and faculty decisions (not tested)

redesign_note: Broad integration framework; no specific assessment redesign.

title: Generative AI and Academic Research: A Review of the Policies from Selected HEIs
authors: Navreet Kaur Rana
source_used: OpenAlex abstract (api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1177/23476311241303800); no legal OA copy found
ft_reason: Review of HEI and publisher policies on GenAI in academic research and authorship; not about student assessment (Amendment 3: c).
sample: Purposively selected HEIs and major publishers (number not given in abstract)

key_findings.finding: HEIs take varied stances on GenAI in research; citing GenAI as an author or in acknowledgements raises integrity questions because tools carry no ethical liability.

limitations: Purposive, website-based policy sample; abstract only.
redesign_note: Research-publication policy; no student assessment redesign content.

title: From integrity to identity: course-level generative AI governance and scholarly subject formation in graduate education
authors: Evelyn Wu
source_used: Frontiers PDF (oa_url)
ft_reason: HE graduate education; analyses course-level GenAI use rules in syllabi and how students interpret them in their work; peer reviewed 2026.
study_design: Bounded interpretive case study (syllabus document analysis and interviews)
discipline: Graduate-intensive college (education/social sciences), US research university
sample: 22 graduate course syllabi and 11 doctoral student interviews

key_findings.finding: Syllabi showed four course-level governance regimes (prohibitionist integrity, conditional authorisation, assistive-generative boundary protection, integration-as-pedagogy), giving students an inconsistent patchwork of rules.
Nine of eleven students (all multilingual) treated AI as acceptable for language assistance but not for intellectual authorship.

dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Distinctions between editing, brainstorming, drafting and authorship need to be explicit at task level.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Multilingual writers experience GenAI as both support and stigma.

author_recommendations: Align course AI rules with assessment design so each assignment's intended intellectual labour is clear (not tested)
limitations: One college and a small purposive self-report sample (Sec 5 limitations).

quality.note: Clear qualitative design with stated limitations.

redesign_note: Shows how permitted-use rules are enacted and interpreted, which informs task-level AI-use declarations.
